summary:
Muninn is a public, browser-based viewer for NASA SPHEREx images that shows what changes in a patch of sky between visits. It reads SPHEREx Level-2 frames straight from NASA's public archive mirror, a few megabytes at a time, puts every visit on a north-up grid, and lets anyone blink, wipe, subtract or stack them. Click any spot and Muninn re-measures it in every visit: does it stay, move or appear once, how bright is it at each wavelength, and what is it, according to Gaia, WISE, 2MASS, SIMBAD and the known asteroids and comets at the moment of each exposure. Hunter X ranks moving candidates across the whole field.

This answers the challenge directly. Planet X would be a faint, slow mover, so the tool is built to find movers, name the known ones, reject false detections such as cosmic rays, and say honestly how deep a single visit reaches compared with the predicted brightness of Planet X. It works on phones, in English and Russian, and in VR, where the field surrounds you and its objects stand at their real distances.

It matters because SPHEREx's all-sky data become something anyone can explore and check, not only specialists.
details:
Overview

Muninn is a public website for seeing how a patch of sky changes between NASA SPHEREx visits. Type a name or coordinates, or pick a star on the sky map, and every SPHEREx visit of that patch appears in time order on one north-up grid, ready to be blinked, wiped, subtracted, stacked, measured and identified. It reads the calibrated Level-2 frames of Data Release 1 and Quick Release 3 straight from NASA's public archive mirror, in the browser, a few megabytes at a time. Nothing is installed, and no pixels are copied to our server.

SPHEREx photographs the whole sky in 102 near-infrared bands, 0.75–5 µm, about twice a year, so most positions have several dates. Stars stay put between those dates; asteroids, comets and anything else bound to the Sun do not. Blinking two dates is how Clyde Tombaugh found Pluto in 1930. Muninn applies that method to an all-sky infrared survey and adds a measurement of any point in every visit, so that what the eye notices can be checked.

The name comes from Norse myth: Odin's two ravens flew over the worlds every day and came back at evening to tell him what had changed. The second was Muninn, "Memory".

- Live site: https://muninn.mydevbox.xyz (open "(152) Atala" under the search; the blink starts on its own)

- Talk: https://muninn.mydevbox.xyz/talk.html (ten slides and an appendix; slide 2 reads real frames as you watch)

- Team Yggdrasil:

Khurshiddinov Timur Khurshiddinovich (team owner)

Stepan Ionichev

Muhammadyusuf Bahtiyarov

Temur Kholjigitov

Khamidkhodjayeva Fayziya

In short, on real data it finds and names a mover (asteroid (152) Atala, SNR 374 in one visit of fifteen), refuses a false discovery (a "flash" of SNR 140 that the pipeline had flagged as a cosmic ray), and measures how far SPHEREx is from Planet Nine (17.61 AB per visit against a prediction of V 22.6–24.3). Each of these is set out with its numbers below.

The science: Planet X and what SPHEREx can add

Planet Nine is a proposed planet of roughly 5–10 Earth masses, put forward by Batygin & Brown (2016) to explain the clustering of the orbits of distant Kuiper Belt objects. The semi-major axes that reproduce the clustering are 400–800 AU (Batygin et al. 2019, Phys. Rep. 805, 1); Brown & Batygin (2021, AJ 162, 219) later put it nearer, about 380 AU, with an inclination of 16 ± 5°. Linder & Mordasini (2016, A&A 589, A134) predict its brightness near aphelion at V 22.6–24.3 for 5–50 Earth masses, and V 21.7 for 10 Earth masses at 700 AU.

Most of a distant body's apparent motion is the Earth's own motion reflected back. At opposition the rate is about 2π · 206265 / (d + √d) arcseconds per year at a distance of d AU: about 34″ per hour in the main belt, 4″ per hour at Neptune, and 0.18–0.35″ per hour for Planet X at 400–800 AU. SPHEREx looks about 90° from the Sun, where the same body drifts only 0.006–0.02″ per hour. Half a year later, with the Earth across its orbit, it has jumped by about 2/d radians: 22.9′ at 300 AU, 13.8′ at 500 AU, 3.4′ at 2000 AU.

This sets what SPHEREx can and cannot do. Its strengths are coverage (the whole sky, twice a year, now public) and colour (102 bands, so anything found also gets a spectrum). Its limit is depth: one visit reaches about 17.6 AB, far brighter than the predicted planet. Muninn is built around both facts. It lets anyone search SPHEREx for things that move or change, and it measures and states, field by field, how deep that search goes.

What it does and how it works

Reading the data

- Pixels. A SPHEREx Level-2 file is a 65–72 MB FITS file, mostly a PSF cube; the 2040 × 2040 flux plane is near the front. NASA's mirror on Amazon Web Services answers HTTP Range requests, so the browser reads only the headers, the detector rows the field lands on, and the same rows of the quality plane: 1–3 MB per visit.

- The frame index comes from NASA/IPAC's Infrared Science Archive (IRSA) Simple Image Access service, four collections of DR1 and QR3. IRSA sends no CORS headers for it, so our small server relays the query and caches the answer. Image data never passes through the server.

- Coordinates. Each frame's own TAN-SIP coordinate solution is built in the browser, and every visit is resampled onto one tangent grid, north up and east left. SPHEREx rolls between visits (the Atala field's December and July frames are 180° apart), so without this a blink would show only rotation. Checked against a live header, the round-trip error is at most 0.015 pixel.

- Quality flags. The Rice-compressed FLAGS plane is decoded in the browser, and before anything is measured every pixel flagged as a cosmic-ray jump, a processing error, dead, hot or cold, missing data, persistence, crosstalk, a satellite streak, a "snowball" particle shower or the halo around such a hit is blanked: eleven flag bits in all. Saturated pixels and optical ghosts are deliberately kept in the picture and carried in a separate quality plane, so a mark on a saturated core says "saturated" and quotes no brightness, and a mark on a ghost is not measured.

- Wavelength. SPHEREx observes through a linear variable filter, so the wavelength depends on where a point falls on the detector. Muninn reads each file's WCS-WAVE table and knows at which wavelength each visit saw each point.

- Loading. Ten visits spread over the whole baseline come first; the rest load in the background, widest time gaps first, up to sixty (thirty on a phone).

Comparing visits

- Blink: the visits play in turn; anything that moves jumps.

- Wipe: two visits either side of a divider you drag.

- Difference: one visit minus the other, violet where A is brighter and amber where B is. The page prints the wavelength each frame saw and warns when the two channels overlap by less than half, since the residual may then be spectrum rather than change. "Pick B at A's wavelength" chooses the visit whose channel overlaps A's most.

- Single: hold one visit.

- Stack: one season's visits in one band, each first put on the same sky level, combined as the median of three or the mean without the brightest for four or more, which removes a missed cosmic ray or a passing asteroid. The page states the depth gained.

- The run strip shows every visit on a time axis, with a 5 × 4 grid of sectors under each, scored as (peak in this visit − median peak across visits) / noise. It is labelled as an attention map, not a detector.

- Beside SPHEREx, as B of the wipe: the AllWISE picture of 2010–2011 on the same grid (the idea of WiseView, which the challenge names), or a "Gaia sky": Gaia DR3 sources carried by proper motion to the visit's date and blurred to SPHEREx's own measured width (FWHM 6.6″ in D1 to 9.9″ in D6). Gaia has no images, so this one is labelled as a model; what SPHEREx shows and the model lacks is what Gaia does not account for.

- Overlays of Gaia DR3 and AllWISE positions; four stretches, three colour ramps, and per-visit or shared brightness scaling, with a note that the first shows motion and hides brightness change and the second does the opposite.

Measuring a point

Click any spot and Muninn re-measures it in every loaded visit: background and noise from a ring, the brightest pixel within ±2 detector pixels, a flux-weighted centre, and the light in a 3 × 3-pixel aperture in AB magnitude and millijanskys. A detection needs 5σ, where σ is never below the noise of the detector pixels themselves. The verdict is one of: nothing above the noise; there on one date only; in N of M visits; in all visits, steady to X″; moving at X″ per hour (three or more detections and motion beyond both one 6.15″ pixel and twice the fit's scatter), with the farthest distance that rate allows; or saturated, with nothing quoted.

A one-visit flash is also tested for sharpness on the detector's own pixels: a star spreads its light over several pixels, a cosmic ray puts it in one. A flash too sharp for a star is labelled so and never ranked.

Each mark asks SIMBAD, Gaia DR3, 2MASS, AllWISE, CatWISE2020 (whether the source moved over ten years of WISE/NEOWISE) and the AAVSO Variable Star Index what is there, and asks NASA/JPL Small-Body Identification and SkyBoT (IMCCE) for known asteroids and comets at the moment of each exposure. A light curve shows brightness visit by visit with error bars.

The spectrum of a point

Each exposure sees a point at its own wavelength, so a year of exposures adds up to a low-resolution spectrum. "Spectrum" looks up the wavelengths of up to 160 exposures and measures up to 60: detections with 1σ bars, non-detections as 5σ limits, saturated exposures as triangles, at the published resolving power R = 39, 41, 41, 35, 112 and 128 for D1–D6 (Crill et al. 2020). Within one resolution element the filter has not changed, so flux against date there is a true light curve, reported as a change past 3σ or "steady within ±Y mag". For a body seen once, only the exposures of that pass are used: (152) Atala gave 22 mJy at 1.5 µm falling to 5 mJy at 4.3 µm. This answers the challenge's call for spectra generated on the fly.

Searching for a distant mover

- Hunter X takes the strongest twelve sector standouts, measures each in every visit with the same photometry as a mark, and ranks what moves, slowest first, since a slower rate can mean a greater distance; known asteroids rank below unknown ones. A candidate is ranked only when its rate is a measurement: four or more detections, total motion over three times the larger of the scatter and one pixel, at most 60″ per hour, and not a one-pixel hit. One-visit flashes are listed separately and checked against SkyBoT. The page calls it a candidate ranking, not a detector, and the benchmark below shows why.

- Link across seasons places a body on the mark's line of sight at 30 to 2000 AU and draws where the Earth's motion puts it in the next season: a parallax arc with ticks at 50, 100, 200, 500 and 1000 AU. It keeps a 5σ source on the arc only if that spot was empty all through the first season, and with two or more visits needs one trial distance to fit at least two. The body's own orbital motion (58″ in half a year at 500 AU) is allowed as a disc, so the answer is a range: "candidate link, check by eye: d ≈ X AU", or "nothing along the arc down to the one-visit limit".

- The depth panel measures each field's 5σ one-visit limit from its own pixels, sets it against the Planet X prediction, and counts the fields and square degrees examined in this browser, so a null result has a stated depth and area.

Getting the result out, and finding a field

A mark's measurements download as CSV (one row per exposure, with wavelength, flux, error, limit and SNR), the plate as PNG, the blink as WebM. The address carries field, size, band, mode, overlay, visit and marks, so a copied link reproduces the view and the tool can be embedded. The search takes names (SIMBAD, NED), catalogue numbers (Gaia DR3, TIC, 2MASS, HD, HIP), planet names, asteroids and comets through JPL, and coordinates in any common form. The way in is a sky map of 15,568 catalogue stars, the Messier objects and today's planets, each with a card showing a real SPHEREx frame of that place.

A typical session

1. Open the site and pick "(152) Atala". The field opens and the blink starts while the other visits load.

2. On one frame a point appears at the centre and is gone in the next; that visit's sector in the run strip lights up.

3. Click the point. The mark reads "there on 25 Dec 2025 and in none of the other visits", and SkyBoT names it at that exposure: (152) Atala.

4. Hunter X lists the flash separately and names it. The depth panel shows what one visit here could have shown, and how far that is from Planet X.

5. Switch to Difference and press "Pick B at A's wavelength" to compare like with like.

6. Press "Spectrum": one to four minutes later the asteroid's spectrum from 0.75 to 5 µm appears.

7. Put AllWISE as B of the wipe to see the field fifteen years earlier.

8. Copy the link or the CSV and send it on; the link opens the same view.

The first field of a page load starts a guided tour; "Not clear" on any step opens a small demo. "How to read this" is sixteen short cards, fourteen of them with a demo (drag the wipe, tap a star, slide a magnitude against the depth bar).

The challenge targets, one by one

Each opens in one press from "Challenge targets", with its frame index shipped in the page and the target ringed on the plate, moved by its catalogue proper motion to each visit's date. A star must cross one 6.15″ pixel to be seen to move.

- Barnard's Star (10.4″ per year; 17 D2 visits over 397 days). It would move 11.3″, but at J ≈ 5 it saturates in every visit and the pipeline blanks its core, so a mark reads "saturated" and states the catalogue motion against the pixel instead. Against AllWISE in the wipe its motion is plain, about 157″ from 2010 to 2025. The other-archives panel lists 572 NEOSSat frames of it from 2019.

- ε Indi B (a pair of brown dwarfs beside ε Indi A; 29 D2 visits over 526 days). Blink in D2, then D6.

- WISE 0855−0714 (the coldest known brown dwarf, 8.1″ per year; 17 D6 visits over 370 days). It opens in D6, the only band it is bright in, centred at its position for the mean date of its visits, 2.1′ west of the challenge's 2010.6 WISE position (motion from Kirkpatrick et al. 2021). At W2 ≈ 13.9, about 17.2 AB, it is below the one-visit D6 limit of 16.7 AB: a test of the Stack, as the page says.

- RW Aurigae (a young irregular variable; 16 D2 visits over 372 days). Shared scaling, then blink. It saturates in this band, so no brightness is quoted.

- R Draconis (a Mira near the north ecliptic pole; 55 D3 visits over 414 days, index capped by the archive). Shared scaling, season by season. It saturates too.

For unsaturated variables a mark gives an AB magnitude per visit; since each visit sees a slightly different wavelength, a Mira's swing shows and a few tenths do not, and the mark says so.

Validation and testing

The Atala field, visit by visit

RA 13.4194, Dec +3.8459, band D2 (1.10–1.65 µm), fifteen visits over 369 days. Peak signal-to-noise at the field centre: 1.2, 2.0, 0.5 and 1.6 (July 2025); 2.2 on 24 December and 374.3 on 25 December 2025; 1.5, 0.9, 2.4 and 0.8 (January 2026); 1.9, 1.4, 1.3, 1.2 and 0.9 (July 2026). On 25 December SkyBoT places (152) Atala, V = 13.81, 2.3″ from the centre at that exposure's timestamp. Before Muninn read FLAGS, 6 July 2025 showed SNR 140 at the same spot: one pixel at eleven times its neighbours, flagged 0x45 in DR1 (TRANSIENT, SUR_ERROR, NONFUNC). With the flags read, it is background like the rest.

The depth, derived

The depth comes from delivered pixels, not a mission number: the robust noise of one detector pixel after FLAGS (median minus 15.87th percentile), through the solid angle of a 6.15″ pixel (8.890 × 10⁻¹⁰ sr), summed over a 3 × 3 aperture, times five, in AB. 17.61 AB corresponds to about 0.0246 MJy/sr, what the Atala D2 visits show (0.0239–0.0248); the pipeline's variance plane gives about 0.022, so this estimate is about 0.1 mag cautious. The page and the measurement script use the same code.

One visit at 5σ, Atala field, by band: D1 17.59, D2 17.61, D3 17.80, D4 18.04 (deepest), D5 17.11, D6 16.68 AB (shallowest). With √N coadding, 10 visits would reach 18.86, 100 visits 20.11, 200 visits 20.49; these extrapolate one-visit noise and are not measured stacks. Against V 22.6–24.3, one visit is 5.0–6.7 magnitudes short (about 99–480 times in flux), 200 visits 2.1–3.8 short, and even against V 21.7, 1.2 short. There is no aperture correction (0.1–0.4 mag), and comparing V with AB at 1.2–1.6 µm is a best case. So Muninn does not find Planet Nine, and says so on screen.

Hunter X injection–recovery benchmark

Fake movers with the frames' own PSF width (1.21 detector pixels) were planted into real DR1 D2 frames of a sparse field (Atala, galactic latitude −59°) and a crowded one (RW Aurigae, −6°), with 4, 6 or 10 visits and also beside real bright stars, and run through the page's own search code, blind.

- In the range asked (peak SNR 5–20, 1–10 pixels of motion), Hunter X returned 1 of 5,184 planted movers as moving.

- The loss is in candidate selection: a slow mover stays in its sector, so it is in the median, and a faint one is below the sector's brightest star. The sector matrix pointed at none of the movers at SNR 20 or below.

- The photometry works in a narrow window: handed the true position, it calls 60 % of SNR 20 movers of 3–5 pixels "moving". At 10 pixels or more the seasons fall outside its ±2-pixel box.

- Within 3 pixels of a brighter star, the photometry follows the star instead.

- False positives are not the problem: 2 ranked false entries in 17,136 runs, and nothing ranked in fields with nothing planted.

So a Planet X–like body would appear as a one-visit flash or "comes and goes", never as a ranked mover; that case is what Link across seasons is for. No code defect was found; every miss follows from a rule working as written. The full tables are in docs/hunter-benchmark.md.

Other checks

- Season link: checked on a synthetic two-season sky only. A source at 300 AU links at 300 AU (range 269–321); a star on the arc and a one-visit peak link nothing.

- Sharpness: over every Atala visit, 932 unflagged stars above 15σ never put more than 0.87 of their 3 × 3 light in one pixel; flagged hits sit at 0.93–1.0, the 6 July pixel at 1.00, Atala at 0.42. The test is applied only from about 57σ.

- Photometry: a constant 12th-magnitude star holds within 0.3 mag over ten visits.

- Independent check: a notebook following the SPHEREx Tutorial Notebooks and the CSA's NEOSSat Data Tutorial reads the same frames with astropy. Its FLAGS bit counts match the header totals, so Muninn's Rice decoder agrees; it confirms the 6 July pixel (0x45, 11.2 times its neighbours), Atala by SkyBoT, and the 572 NEOSSat frames. Its signal-to-noise is 10–20 % higher (425 against 374 for Atala), because it reads the peak on detector pixels rather than the resampled grid; the conclusions do not change.

- Automated tests: 245 offline tests, about five seconds, run on every push and pull request: a synthetic FITS through the whole pipeline, a real DR1 FLAGS row, the real pixels of the 6 July hit and of Atala, WCS, photometry, saturation, stack, season link, spectrum and server.

Limitations, stated plainly

- Released data only: DR1 (April 2025 to mid-May 2026) and QR3 (mid-May to early October 2026). Coverage is uneven; some positions return nothing.

- The archive caps a query at 500 frames per collection; the page says when a list is truncated.

- Brightness is not comparable across bands, and within a band each visit sees a slightly different wavelength.

- The spectrum is built over up to a year, not taken at once, in a 3 × 3 aperture with no aperture correction.

- Light-curve errors are detector noise plus a 0.03 mag floor; a change near 3σ is worth checking by eye.

- The photometry is simple aperture photometry on the resampled grid, not PSF photometry.

- Hunter X has a narrow window, and inside an eleven-day season its motion test is blind at Planet X distances (0.006–0.02″ per hour against a threshold of 0.07″). The season link is checked only on synthetic data.

- Known-object matches are geocentric; SPHEREx's orbit shifts a main-belt asteroid by 3–7″, inside the match radius.

- A distance from a rate is a ceiling assuming a circular orbit in the ecliptic, not an orbit.

- Cosmic rays the pipeline missed are caught by the sharpness test only from about 57σ.

- Most nearby brown dwarfs move too slowly to cross a pixel over the 1.2-year baseline.

- Planet X by its brightness is out of reach: 5.0–6.7 magnitudes per visit.

Data provenance

- SPHEREx Level-2 images, DR1 and QR3: NASA/JPL-Caltech and IPAC/IRSA, via the AWS Open Data mirror nasa-irsa-spherex; frame index from IRSA Simple Image Access; FLAGS and WCS-WAVE from the same files.

- AllWISE Atlas images (W1, W2) through IRSA; AllWISE, CatWISE2020, 2MASS and Gaia DR3 catalogues through IRSA TAP, raced against CDS VizieR and its CfA mirror; one Gaia star through NASA MAST.

- Known asteroids and comets: NASA/JPL Small-Body Identification with SkyBoT (IMCCE); names typed in, NASA/JPL SBDB and Horizons.

- Planet hosts: the NASA Exoplanet Archive (4,862 hosts). Other telescopes of the field, NEOSSat included: the Canadian Astronomy Data Centre.

- Outside NASA: SIMBAD, Sesame and AAVSO VSX through CDS Strasbourg; Bailer-Jones et al. 2021 distances for VR.

From the challenge's Resources tab: IRSA for pixels, index and flags (its SPHEREx cutout service was measured and not used: 4 MB and 13–21 s a frame, against 1–3 MB in a few seconds by range request); the SPHEREx Tutorial Notebooks for the file layout and the astropy check; WiseView as the model for the AllWISE wipe; Gaia DR3; CADC and NEOSSat. Muninn is not affiliated with NASA and adds nothing to the data it shows. The code is MIT-licensed.

Performance

- 1–3 MB per visit from a 65–72 MB file; six frames at once, four on modest devices.

- A spectrum: wavelengths of up to 160 exposures (about 70 KB each), then up to 60 measured (about 0.3 MB each), in one to four minutes with progress shown.

- Code and indexes are pre-compressed: a 390 KB field index travels as 40 KB.

- The server caches archive answers for 12 hours and visit lists for 30 days, serving the last list when IRSA fails.

- VR asks a headset for 90 Hz when a frame's work takes 9 ms or less, otherwise 72 Hz. In a Quest 3 emulator on a desktop GPU the median frame took about 7 ms with 54 draw calls; it has not yet been timed on a physical headset.

Benefits

- Real NASA data, not illustrations: pixels read from the archive as you look, with the pipeline's own flags applied, and every identification naming its catalogue.

- Nothing to install; a link opens it on a laptop, phone or headset and reproduces the exact view.

- It refuses false discoveries: flagged pixels masked, single-pixel flashes labelled, saturated stars quoting nothing, the depth of each search stated.

- It keeps working when services fail: each catalogue is raced across mirrors (25 s at most), one that fails is named with a retry, and the ten ready fields ship with their indexes and open on any static host.

- Ready for new releases: a new SPHEREx release is one line in one file, a re-bake and a deploy. That is how Muninn moved from QR2 to DR1 and QR3 on 13 November 2026.

Intended impact

SPHEREx's all-sky data should be explorable by students, amateur astronomers, teachers and the public, not only by specialists with Python pipelines. Blinking for movers has a record of volunteer discovery in WISE data through WiseView and Backyard Worlds; Muninn aims to give SPHEREx the same kind of public, check-it-yourself tool, with a measurement behind every look.

It also teaches the method and its honesty. In the Atala field a visitor sees, within a minute, a real discovery-style event, its identification, and a false alarm explained by the data's own flags. The depth panel then shows why a Planet X search with this survey is a search for upper limits, which is itself a result when stated with its depth and area. For researchers it is a quick look at any SPHEREx position across time and wavelength, with per-exposure CSV and a reproducible link. The bilingual interface and the Russian study guide aim it at classrooms too.

Tools, coding languages, hardware and software

- Front end: JavaScript modules, HTML and CSS, no framework and no build step; our own FITS, Rice and TAN-SIP readers in the browser and Web Workers.

- Server: a dependency-free Node.js relay with fixed query templates, input checks, rate limits, caching and a content-security policy naming every origin. No secrets; every archive is open.

- VR: three.js over WebXR, Meta Quest 3 first; sound synthesised with the Web Audio API.

- Verification: Node's test runner in GitHub Actions; measurement and benchmark scripts in the repository; a Jupyter notebook with astropy, astroquery and pyvo.

- Hosting: a small Android TV box at home behind a Cloudflare Tunnel; the images come from NASA's AWS mirror. A static fallback deploys with one edge function.

- Git and GitHub, with issues and pull requests.

How it is creative

- A 1930s discovery technique in a web browser on a 2025–2026 all-sky infrared survey; the day theme even draws frames as photographic negatives, as plates were blinked.

- A spectrum of any point from a year of visits, turning SPHEREx's linear variable filter, usually a complication, into one button.

- Reading only the bytes that matter, so a phone can work with real survey files.

- A parallax arc as a search tool: a mark in one season becomes a curve of predicted positions in the next, with distance ticks.

- A Gaia model sky beside the real frame, labelled as a model, so that what Gaia does not explain stands out.

- A VR view where the flat image unfolds into real depth, so two "neighbours" on the image turn out to be thousands of light years apart.

Beyond the challenge: VR and ExoVision

In VR (any WebXR headset, or a computer with the mouse) you stand inside the sky of 15,568 catalogue stars. Point at a star to open its field, and its visits surround you on screens you can grab and resize; marks use the same code as the website. Behind you the field stands in depth: Gaia stars by distance, known asteroids at their distance on each visit's date, galaxies by redshift, and labelled shells for Neptune, the predicted Planet X zone (400–800 AU), the Oort cloud and the Galactic centre. You can fly to an object, measure the distance between two, show a path, and run stellar motion 10,000 years either way. Limits are said in the scene: without radial velocities the stars move across the sky but not toward or away, and a field far from the ecliptic is told that Planet X is not expected there. Sound is synthesised: air that follows your flight, soft interface tones, and a chosen star whose pitch follows its B−V colour, a sonification of catalogue numbers labelled as such.

A star with known planets within 90″ offers its system in ExoVision, the team's exoplanet explorer, and links back.

What our team considered

- Honesty first. Every number on the page is measured from the pixels or cited. Planet X is fainter than a visit can see, and the page says by how much. Hunter X is a ranking, and the benchmark showing its narrow window ships with the code. Where the data hold no value, such as a saturated core or a missing colour, the interface says so rather than drawing a number.

- Correctness. Early versions were reviewed against the code and fixed where they fell short: flags not yet read (the 6 July flash), mirrored frames, a depth from the smoothed grid about 0.4 mag too deep, and a distance bound pointing the wrong way. Tests now hold each fix.

- The challenge text. A field entered as RA/Dec plays "like a little video", and each optional consideration has an answer: new releases in one line, the bands plus an on-the-fly spectrum, adding and subtracting dates, a chosen field of view (0.1° to 0.6°), Gaia and WISE overlays and images, coordinates in the URL, the pipeline's contamination flags, and Astropy in the independent check.

- Weak devices: fewer frames at once, no run animation while loading, thirty visits on phones.

- Reach: English and Russian; day and night themes; 44-pixel touch targets; reduced motion respected; layouts from 320-pixel phones to headsets; keyboard control.

- Colour as information: a grey plate whose brightness never changes with hue, colour ramps rising steadily in luminance, and chrome tinted by the band in view.

- Responsible use of NASA services: small range reads, caching, merging of identical questions, a polite rate, a named User-Agent, and no stored pixels.

Future work

- Measure Hunter X on motion within one season and on jumps of hundreds of pixels between seasons, the cases the benchmark did not test, and let it follow a mover beyond its fixed ±2-pixel box.

- Let the sector score see a faint newcomer beside a brighter steady star.

- Test the season link on real frames with injected distant bodies.

- Add aperture correction and PSF photometry.

- Follow each new SPHEREx release: the coadded depth and the upper limit over the examined area improve with every visit.
